claim: TCR signal strength exerts opposite and hierarchical effects on the balance of Th1 and Tfh cells responding to acute versus persistent infection.
source: We found that TCR signal strength exerts opposite and hierarchical effects on the balance of Th1 and Tfh cells responding to acute versus persistent infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CD4 T cell differentiation in response to acute (Armstrong) versus chronic (Clone-13) LCMV infection with altered peptide ligands.

claim: TCR signal strength correlates positively with Th1 generation during acute infection.
source: TCR signal strength correlates positively with Th1 generation during acute but negatively during chronic infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased Th1:Tfh ratios with stronger TCR signals during Armstrong infection (Figure 2D).

claim: TCR signal strength correlates negatively with Th1 generation during chronic infection.
source: TCR signal strength correlates positively with Th1 generation during acute but negatively during chronic infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing decreased Th1:Tfh ratios with stronger TCR signals during Clone-13 infection (Figure 3D).

claim: Weakly activated T cells express lower levels of markers associated with chronic T cell stimulation.
source: Weakly activated T cells express lower levels of markers associated with chronic T cell stimulation and may resist functional inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing decreased PD1 and Lag3 expression on SMARTA T cells responding to weaker TCR signals during Clone-13 infection (Figure 4A-D).

claim: Viral infection induces the early bifurcation of CD4 T cells into Th1 and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells.
source: Viral infection induces the early bifurcation of CD4 T cells into Th1 and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CD4 T cell differentiation during viral infection.

claim: Th1 cells potentiate CD8 T cell and macrophage cytotoxicity.
source: Th1 cells potentiate CD8 T cell and macrophage cytotoxicity, whereas Tfh cells support antibody production by providing survival and proliferation signals to B cells (Zhu et al., 2010; Crotty, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on Th1 cell function.

claim: Tfh cells support antibody production by providing survival and proliferation signals to B cells.
source: Th1 cells potentiate CD8 T cell and macrophage cytotoxicity, whereas Tfh cells support antibody production by providing survival and proliferation signals to B cells (Zhu et al., 2010; Crotty, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on Tfh cell function.

claim: The cumulative strength of interaction between TCR and pMHC has a clear impact on T cell expansion and fitness.
source: Although the cumulative strength of interaction between TCR and pMHC has a clear impact on T cell expansion and fitness, its influence on the acquisition of Th1 and Tfh cell fates is controversial (Keck et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2019; Snook et al., 2018; DiToro et al., 2018; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011; Fazilleau et al., 2009; Vanguri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating the impact of TCR-pMHC interaction strength on T cell expansion.

claim: The influence of TCR signal strength on the acquisition of Th1 and Tfh cell fates is controversial.
source: Although the cumulative strength of interaction between TCR and pMHC has a clear impact on T cell expansion and fitness, its influence on the acquisition of Th1 and Tfh cell fates is controversial (Keck et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2019; Snook et al., 2018; DiToro et al., 2018; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011; Fazilleau et al., 2009; Vanguri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies with conflicting findings on TCR signal strength and T cell fate.

claim: Distinct TCRs induce reproducible and biased patterns of Th1 and Tfh phenotypes.
source: The authors observed that distinct TCRs induced reproducible and biased patterns of Th1 and Tfh phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to a study by Tubo et al., 2013 that assessed phenotypes of progeny from individual TCR transgenic T cells.

claim: Tfh cells develop across a wide range of signal strengths.
source: Although earlier reports suggested that Tfh cell differentiation requires high TCR signal strength, recent work supports the idea that Tfh cells develop across a wide range of signal strengths, while increasing TCR signal intensity favors Th1 generation (Keck et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2019; Snook et al., 2018; DiToro et al., 2018; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011; Fazilleau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on Tfh cell differentiation.

claim: Increasing TCR signal intensity favors Th1 generation.
source: Although earlier reports suggested that Tfh cell differentiation requires high TCR signal strength, recent work supports the idea that Tfh cells develop across a wide range of signal strengths, while increasing TCR signal intensity favors Th1 generation (Keck et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2019; Snook et al., 2018; DiToro et al., 2018; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011; Fazilleau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on Th1 cell differentiation.

claim: Persistent TCR signaling drives a shift toward Tfh differentiation during chronic infection.
source: Although existing reports suggest that persistent TCR signaling drives a shift toward Tfh differentiation during chronic infection, whether this outcome can be modulated by TCR signal strength has not been examined (Oxenius et al., 1998; Fahey et al., 2011; Crawford et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CD4 T cell differentiation during chronic infection.

claim: The use of MHC-II tetramers to track endogenous polyclonal T cell responses does not adequately detect low affinity T cells.
source: The use of MHC-II tetramers to track endogenous polyclonal T cell responses does not adequately detect low affinity T cells that can comprise up to 50% of an effector response in autoimmune or viral infection settings (Sabatino et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on MHC-II tetramer detection limitations.

claim: Low affinity T cells can comprise up to 50% of an effector response in autoimmune or viral infection settings.
source: The use of MHC-II tetramers to track endogenous polyclonal T cell responses does not adequately detect low affinity T cells that can comprise up to 50% of an effector response in autoimmune or viral infection settings (Sabatino et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on the composition of effector T cell responses.

claim: 75 altered peptide ligands (APLs) for the SMARTA TCR transgenic line were identified using CD69 as a proxy for TCR signal strength.
source: Using the early activation marker CD69 as a proxy for TCR signal strength, we identified 75 APLs for the SMARTA TCR tg line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary materials.

claim: Blocking IFNAR had no effect on CD69 expression at 6 hr after activation.
source: Blocking interferon-a receptor (IFNAR) had no effect on CD69 expression at 6 hr after activation, while a CD25 and IRF4 were modestly decreased in SMARTA T cells activated with low-dose APL, suggesting that the activation hierarchy of these APLs is mainly a result of differences in TCR signal strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from IFN type-I blocking experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD25 and IRF4 were modestly decreased in SMARTA T cells activated with low-dose APL when IFNAR was blocked.
source: Blocking interferon-a receptor (IFNAR) had no effect on CD69 expression at 6 hr after activation, while a CD25 and IRF4 were modestly decreased in SMARTA T cells activated with low-dose APL, suggesting that the activation hierarchy of these APLs is mainly a result of differences in TCR signal strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from IFN type-I blocking experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The activation hierarchy of APLs is mainly a result of differences in TCR signal strength.
source: Blocking interferon-a receptor (IFNAR) had no effect on CD69 expression at 6 hr after activation, while a CD25 and IRF4 were modestly decreased in SMARTA T cells activated with low-dose APL, suggesting that the activation hierarchy of these APLs is mainly a result of differences in TCR signal strength.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IFNAR blocking experiments showing minimal effects on CD69 expression.

claim: Five APL-encoding sequences were successfully introduced into the genomes of both LCMV Armstrong and Clone-13.
source: Five APL-encoding sequences were successfully introduced into the genomes of both LCMV Armstrong (Armstrong variants) and Clone-13 (Clone-13 variants), the latter of which contains a mutation in the polymerase gene L that enhances the replicative capacity of the virus, enabling viral persistence (Bergthaler et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on virus generation using site-directed mutagenesis.

claim: Clone-13 contains a mutation in the polymerase gene L that enhances the replicative capacity of the virus, enabling viral persistence.
source: Five APL-encoding sequences were successfully introduced into the genomes of both LCMV Armstrong (Armstrong variants) and Clone-13 (Clone-13 variants), the latter of which contains a mutation in the polymerase gene L that enhances the replicative capacity of the virus, enabling viral persistence (Bergthaler et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing the Clone-13 virus.

claim: V71S and Y72F variants demonstrated comparable viral fitness in vitro and in vivo.
source: Of these viruses, two variants, V71S and Y72F (EC50 ~0.1 and 1 µM, respectively) demonstrated comparable viral fitness in vitro and in vivo, with all three Clone-13 variants persisting in the blood, spleen, and kidney throughout the 21-day observation period (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral growth kinetics and viral load data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: All three Clone-13 variants persisted in the blood, spleen, and kidney throughout the 21-day observation period.
source: Of these viruses, two variants, V71S and Y72F (EC50 ~0.1 and 1 µM, respectively) demonstrated comparable viral fitness in vitro and in vivo, with all three Clone-13 variants persisting in the blood, spleen, and kidney throughout the 21-day observation period (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data over time shown in Figure 1E.

claim: V71S has an EC50 of approximately 0.1 µM.
source: Of these viruses, two variants, V71S and Y72F (EC50 ~0.1 and 1 µM, respectively) demonstrated comparable viral fitness in vitro and in vivo, with all three Clone-13 variants persisting in the blood, spleen, and kidney throughout the 21-day observation period (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide dose-activation curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Y72F has an EC50 of approximately 1 µM.
source: Of these viruses, two variants, V71S and Y72F (EC50 ~0.1 and 1 µM, respectively) demonstrated comparable viral fitness in vitro and in vivo, with all three Clone-13 variants persisting in the blood, spleen, and kidney throughout the 21-day observation period (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide dose-activation curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Comparable viral load was observed across all organs at 21 days post infection in DBA/2 mice.
source: To additionally rule out any contribution of endogenous CD4 T cells to viral control, we also determined the viral load in DBA/2 mice which are unable to present the GP61 epitope. Here, again we observed comparable viral load across all organs at 21 days post infection and in the blood over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data in DBA/2 mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: DBA/2 mice are unable to present the GP61 epitope.
source: To additionally rule out any contribution of endogenous CD4 T cells to viral control, we also determined the viral load in DBA/2 mice which are unable to present the GP61 epitope.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about MHC haplotypes in DBA/2 mice.

claim: GP67-77 is the minimal binding epitope of GP61.
source: Finally, as GP67-77, the minimal binding epitope of GP61, can bind to MHC in different registers, we considered the possibility that V71 and Y72 might act as MHC anchor residues as opposed to TCR contact residues (Homann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the GP61 epitope.

claim: GP67-77 can bind to MHC in different registers.
source: Finally, as GP67-77, the minimal binding epitope of GP61, can bind to MHC in different registers, we considered the possibility that V71 and Y72 might act as MHC anchor residues as opposed to TCR contact residues (Homann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on MHC binding registers.

claim: Comparable binding of APL peptides to MHC-II was observed in the out-competition assay.
source: Here, we observed comparable binding of APL peptides to MHC-II, indicating that reduced activation of SMARTA T cells is unlikely to be a result of V71 and Y72 acting as crucial MHC anchor residues (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by out-competition assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Reduced activation of SMARTA T cells is unlikely to be a result of V71 and Y72 acting as crucial MHC anchor residues.
source: Here, we observed comparable binding of APL peptides to MHC-II, indicating that reduced activation of SMARTA T cells is unlikely to be a result of V71 and Y72 acting as crucial MHC anchor residues (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the out-competition assay results showing comparable MHC-II binding.

claim: All LCMV variants were capable of inducing SMARTA T cell expansion at day 10 post infection.
source: All LCMV variants were capable of inducing SMARTA T cell expansion at day 10 post infection (p.i.), and a direct correlation between TCR signal strength and the number of SMARTA T cells recovered was observed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A direct correlation between TCR signal strength and the number of SMARTA T cells recovered was observed at day 10 post infection.
source: All LCMV variants were capable of inducing SMARTA T cell expansion at day 10 post infection (p.i.), and a direct correlation between TCR signal strength and the number of SMARTA T cells recovered was observed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data showing higher SMARTA numbers with stronger TCR signals in Figure 2A.

claim: Expansion of endogenous LCMV nucleoprotein (NP)-specific T cells was similar across all three viral strains.
source: In contrast, expansion of endogenous LCMV nucleoprotein (NP)-specific as well as antigen-experienced CD44+ T cells was similar across all three viral strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data for NP309+ cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expansion of antigen-experienced CD44+ T cells was similar across all three viral strains.
source: In contrast, expansion of endogenous LCMV nucleoprotein (NP)-specific as well as antigen-experienced CD44+ T cells was similar across all three viral strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data for CD44+ cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expansion hierarchy among the viruses was maintained >30 days after LCMV infection.
source: The expansion hierarchy among the viruses was maintained >30 days after LCMV infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data at >30 days post infection shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Strong T cell stimulation induced a larger proportion of Ly6c+ Th1 effectors during acute infection.
source: Consistent with previous reports, strong T cell stimulation induced a larger proportion of Ly6c+ Th1 effectors, whereas the proportion of Tfh effectors was decreased (Figure 2B–D; Keck et al., 2014; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B-D and citations to previous studies.

claim: The proportion of Tfh effectors was decreased with strong T cell stimulation during acute infection.
source: Consistent with previous reports, strong T cell stimulation induced a larger proportion of Ly6c+ Th1 effectors, whereas the proportion of Tfh effectors was decreased (Figure 2B–D; Keck et al., 2014; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Ploquin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B-D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Differences in SMARTA T cell expansion were observed as early as day 4 after infection.
source: Differences in SMARTA T cell expansion and the proportion of CD25+ Th1 precursor cells were observed as early as day 4 after infection, preceding germinal center responses in both viruses (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data at day 4 post infection shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in the proportion of CD25+ Th1 precursor cells were observed as early as day 4 after infection.
source: Differences in SMARTA T cell expansion and the proportion of CD25+ Th1 precursor cells were observed as early as day 4 after infection, preceding germinal center responses in both viruses (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data at day 4 post infection shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Differences in SMARTA T cell expansion and CD25+ cells preceded germinal center responses in both viruses.
source: Differences in SMARTA T cell expansion and the proportion of CD25+ Th1 precursor cells were observed as early as day 4 after infection, preceding germinal center responses in both viruses (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of T cell changes (day 4) relative to germinal center B cell data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of Bcl6 and T-bet revealed a mild but significant trend toward increased Tbet and decreased Bcl6 in response to strong stimulation.
source: Accordingly, the expression of Bcl6 and T-bet, lineage defining transcription factors for Tfh and Th1 cells, respectively, revealed a mild but significant trend toward increased Tbet and decreased Bcl6 in response to strong stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for transcription factor expression shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bcl6 expression was higher on Tfh compared to Th1 effectors.
source: Importantly, Bcl6 expression was higher on Tfh compared to Th1 effectors, with no differences observed between strong and weak stimulation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing Bcl6 expression in Th1 and Tfh subsets shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No differences in Bcl6 expression were observed between strong and weak stimulation within Tfh and Th1 subsets.
source: Importantly, Bcl6 expression was higher on Tfh compared to Th1 effectors, with no differences observed between strong and weak stimulation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: TCR signal strength is unlikely to exert a qualitative impact on Th1 and Tfh subsets during acute infection.
source: These data indicate that TCR signal strength is unlikely to exert a qualitative impact on these subsets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Bcl6 expression patterns are similar between strong and weak stimulation within each subset.

claim: No impact of TCR signal strength on the development of PSGL1hiLy6clo T cells was observed.
source: Notably, we did not observe any impact of TCR signal strength on the development of PSGL1hiLy6clo T cells, previously reported to be a less differentiated population of Th1 effectors (Figure 2—figure supplement 7; Künzli et al., 2020; Marshall et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: SMARTA T cells responding to chronic LCMV preferentially adopt a Tfh effector phenotype.
source: In contrast to acute LCMV infection, SMARTA T cells responding to chronic LCMV preferentially adopt a Tfh effector phenotype (Fahey et al., 2011; Crawford et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CD4 T cell differentiation during chronic LCMV infection.

claim: The impact of TCR signal strength on CD4 T cell differentiation during chronic infection has not been determined.
source: The impact of TCR signal strength within this context has not been determined, although affinity diversity among endogenous T cells is reportedly similar between acute and chronic LCMV infection (Andargachew et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior studies examining TCR signal strength effects during chronic infection.

claim: Affinity diversity among endogenous T cells is reportedly similar between acute and chronic LCMV infection.
source: The impact of TCR signal strength within this context has not been determined, although affinity diversity among endogenous T cells is reportedly similar between acute and chronic LCMV infection (Andargachew et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing T cell affinity diversity in acute and chronic infection.

claim: SMARTA T cell numbers at day 7 post infection positively correlated with TCR signal strength during Clone-13 infection.
source: Consistent with the results from acute infection, SMARTA T cell numbers at day 7 p.i. positively correlated with TCR signal strength, while the expansion of NP-specific and CD4+CD44+ T cells was similar in response to all three Clone-13 variants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data at day 7 post infection shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expansion of NP-specific and CD4+CD44+ T cells was similar in response to all three Clone-13 variants.
source: Consistent with the results from acute infection, SMARTA T cell numbers at day 7 p.i. positively correlated with TCR signal strength, while the expansion of NP-specific and CD4+CD44+ T cells was similar in response to all three Clone-13 variants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data for NP309+ and CD44+ cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Infection with rLCMV Clone-13 Y72F induced approximately twofold more SMARTA T cell effectors compared to acute infection.
source: Importantly, infection with rLCMV Clone-13 Y72F induced approximately twofold more SMARTA T cell effectors compared to acute infection, allowing for a thorough investigation of T cells responding to this very weak potency variant (Figure 3A, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing cell count data between Figure 3A (Clone-13) and Figure 2A (Armstrong).

claim: Strong TCR stimulation during rLCMV Clone-13 GP61 wt infection shifted the balance toward Tfh effector cell differentiation when compared to strong TCR stimulation in the context of acute infection.
source: With respect to T cell phenotype, strong TCR stimulation during rLCMV Clone-13 GP61 wt infection shifted the balance toward Tfh effector cell differentiation when compared to strong TCR stimulation in the context of acute infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing Th1:Tfh ratios between Armstrong and Clone-13 infections shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Weaker TCR signaling during Clone-13 variant infection resulted in increased proportions of both PSGL1hiLy6chi and PSGL1hiLy6clo Th1 cells.
source: Unexpectedly, and in contrast to the Armstrong variants, weaker TCR signaling during Clone-13 variant infection resulted in increased proportions of both PSGL1hiLy6chi and PSGL1hiLy6clo Th1 cells with the weakest variant, Y72F, generating the highest proportion of Th1 effectors (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The weakest variant, Y72F, generated the highest proportion of Th1 effectors during Clone-13 infection.
source: Unexpectedly, and in contrast to the Armstrong variants, weaker TCR signaling during Clone-13 variant infection resulted in increased proportions of both PSGL1hiLy6chi and PSGL1hiLy6clo Th1 cells with the weakest variant, Y72F, generating the highest proportion of Th1 effectors (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All Clone-13 variants sustained high viral titers in the kidneys at day 7 post infection.
source: The shift toward Th1 effectors in response to lower TCR signal strength is unlikely to be due to differences in antigen load as all variants sustained high viral titers in the kidneys at day 7 p.i. (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data in kidneys shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The shift toward Th1 effectors in response to lower TCR signal strength during Clone-13 infection is unlikely to be due to differences in antigen load.
source: The shift toward Th1 effectors in response to lower TCR signal strength is unlikely to be due to differences in antigen load as all variants sustained high viral titers in the kidneys at day 7 p.i. (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that viral titers are similar across variants despite different Th1:Tfh ratios.

claim: NP-specific CD4 T cells exhibited a similar ratio of Th1 to Tfh effectors across all three Clone-13 infections.
source: In addition, although the viral titer of intermediate potency variant V71S was slightly decreased compared to GP61 wt and Y72F infection, NP-specific CD4 T cells exhibited a similar ratio of Th1 to Tfh effectors across all three infections (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for NP309+ cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The viral titer of intermediate potency variant V71S was slightly decreased compared to GP61 wt and Y72F infection.
source: In addition, although the viral titer of intermediate potency variant V71S was slightly decreased compared to GP61 wt and Y72F infection, NP-specific CD4 T cells exhibited a similar ratio of Th1 to Tfh effectors across all three infections (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Stronger Th1 differentiation was observed at early time points after infection with Clone-13 variant viruses.
source: Similar to LCMV Armstrong infection, stronger Th1 differentiation was also observed at early time points after infection with Clone-13 variant viruses although no differences in germinal center B cell kinetics were observed (Figure 3—figure supplements 6–9).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data at early time points shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 6-9.

claim: No differences in germinal center B cell kinetics were observed after infection with Clone-13 variant viruses.
source: Similar to LCMV Armstrong infection, stronger Th1 differentiation was also observed at early time points after infection with Clone-13 variant viruses although no differences in germinal center B cell kinetics were observed (Figure 3—figure supplements 6–9).
evidence: This claim is supported by germinal center B cell data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: CD25 expression was only weakly and uniformly expressed in all Clone-13 variants at day 4 after infection.
source: In contrast to LCMV Armstrong infection, however, CD25 expression was only weakly and uniformly expressed in all Clone-13 variants at day 4 after infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for CD25 expression shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Lowering the antigen load while maintaining the inflammatory environment caused strongly stimulated SMARTA T cells to expand less and generate a higher proportion of Th1 effectors at day 7 post infection.
source: In response to lowered antigen load, strongly stimulated SMARTA T cells expanded less and generated a higher proportion of Th1 effectors at day 7 p.i. while the expansion and differentiation outcome of weakly activated T cells was antigen load independent (Figure 3—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mixed virus infections shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 10.

claim: The expansion and differentiation outcome of weakly activated T cells was antigen load independent.
source: In response to lowered antigen load, strongly stimulated SMARTA T cells expanded less and generated a higher proportion of Th1 effectors at day 7 p.i. while the expansion and differentiation outcome of weakly activated T cells was antigen load independent (Figure 3—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mixed virus infections shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 10.

claim: Biased Tfh differentiation during Clone-13 GP61 wt infection may be at least partially due to high antigen load.
source: Taken together, these data reveal that TCR signal strength differentially modulates T cell fate acquisition according to the infectious context and that biased Tfh differentiation during Clone-13 GP61 wt infection may be at least partially due to high antigen load.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the antigen dose experiment showing that lowering antigen load increases Th1 differentiation.

claim: T cells start to upregulate inhibitory surface markers associated with chronic activation during Clone-13 infection.
source: During Clone-13 infection, T cells start to upregulate inhibitory surface markers associated with chronic activation, a state often referred to as 'exhaustion' (Crawford et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2019; Mou et al., 2013; Jean Bosco et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T cell exhaustion during chronic infection.

claim: T cells responding to strong TCR signals expressed the highest levels of both PD1 and Lag3 at day 14 post Clone-13 infection.
source: T cells responding to strong TCR signals expressed the highest levels of both PD1 and Lag3, two well characterized co-inhibitory receptors (Figure 4A–B; Crawford et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for PD1 and Lag3 expression shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: SMARTA T cells co-expressing both PD1 and Lag3 were most abundant following Clone-13 GP61 wt infection.
source: SMARTA T cells co-expressing both PD1 and Lag3 were most abundant following Clone-13 GP61 wt infection and decreased in response to Clone-13 variant infection (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for PD1+Lag3+ cells shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: PD1 and Lag3 co-expression decreased in response to Clone-13 variant infection.
source: SMARTA T cells co-expressing both PD1 and Lag3 were most abundant following Clone-13 GP61 wt infection and decreased in response to Clone-13 variant infection (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The basal activation of CD4+CD44+ T cells was equivalent across all three Clone-13 strains at day 14 post infection.
source: Although the viral load was decreased in Clone-13 variant infections at this time point, the basal activation of CD4+CD44+ T cells was equivalent across all three strains and clearly above the recombinant LCMV Armstrong control (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for CD44+ T cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The viral load was decreased in Clone-13 variant infections at day 14 post infection.
source: Although the viral load was decreased in Clone-13 variant infections at this time point, the basal activation of CD4+CD44+ T cells was equivalent across all three strains and clearly above the recombinant LCMV Armstrong control (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMARTA Tfh cells expressed higher levels of TOX compared to Th1 cells in response to acute infection.
source: In response to acute infection, SMARTA Tfh cells expressed higher levels of TOX compared to Th1 cells, consistent with an earlier study highlighting the importance of TOX for Tfh cell development (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for TOX expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TOX expression during rLCMV Clone-13 wt infection was most highly upregulated by Th1 effectors.
source: In contrast, TOX expression during rLCMV Clone-13 wt infection was most highly upregulated by Th1 effectors (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for TOX expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TOX was decreased on SMARTA T cells responding to rLCMV Clone-13 variant viruses.
source: In line with the expression of PD1 and Lag3, TOX was decreased on SMARTA T cells responding to rLCMV Clone-13 variant viruses, despite being comparably induced on CD4+CD44+ T cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for TOX expression shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TOX was comparably induced on CD4+CD44+ T cells across all Clone-13 variants.
source: In line with the expression of PD1 and Lag3, TOX was decreased on SMARTA T cells responding to rLCMV Clone-13 variant viruses, despite being comparably induced on CD4+CD44+ T cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: TOX is important for the survival of stem-like TCF1+ CD8 T cells that accumulate during chronic LCMV.
source: TOX was recently demonstrated to be important for the survival of stem-like TCF1+ CD8 T cells that accumulate during chronic LCMV (Khan et al., 2019; Im et al., 2016; Utzschneider et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on TOX function in CD8 T cells during chronic infection.

claim: TCF1+ CD8 T cells and Tfh cells have transcriptional similarities.
source: Given the transcriptional similarities of TCF1+ CD8 T cells and Tfh cells, we wondered if TCF1 would be similarly regulated by TCR signal strength following Clone-13 variant infection (Vella et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing transcriptional profiles.

claim: TCF1 is similarly expressed by T cells responding to all three rLCMV Clone-13 variants.
source: Here we observed that unlike TOX expression, TCF1 is similarly expressed by T cells responding to all three rLCMV Clone-13 variants (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5), indicating that TCF1 expression is likely to be maintained independently of TCR signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data for TCF1 expression shown in Figure 4F.

claim: TCF1 expression is likely to be maintained independently of TCR signals.
source: Here we observed that unlike TOX expression, TCF1 is similarly expressed by T cells responding to all three rLCMV Clone-13 variants (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5), indicating that TCF1 expression is likely to be maintained independently of TCR signals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TCF1 expression does not vary with TCR signal strength.

claim: The observation that TCR signal intensity correlates with Th1 generation during acute infection is consistent with accumulating evidence that higher potency ligands increase T cell sensitivity to IL-2.
source: The observation that TCR signal intensity correlates with Th1 generation during acute infection is consistent with accumulating evidence that higher potency ligands increase T cell sensitivity to IL-2, which likely drives the survival and expansion of Th1 effectors (Keck et al., 2014; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Fazilleau et al., 2009; Gottschalk et al., 2012; Ploquin et al., 2011; Allison et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on TCR signal strength and IL-2 sensitivity.

claim: Higher potency ligands increase T cell sensitivity to IL-2, which likely drives the survival and expansion of Th1 effectors.
source: The observation that TCR signal intensity correlates with Th1 generation during acute infection is consistent with accumulating evidence that higher potency ligands increase T cell sensitivity to IL-2, which likely drives the survival and expansion of Th1 effectors (Keck et al., 2014; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Tubo et al., 2013; Fazilleau et al., 2009; Gottschalk et al., 2012; Ploquin et al., 2011; Allison et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IL-2 and Th1 cell development.

claim: The paradigm for Th1/Th2 cell differentiation is that stronger signals induce Th1 cells and weaker signals induce Th2 cells.
source: This is similar to the paradigm described for Th1/Th2 cell differentiation, where stronger signals induce Th1 cells and weaker signals induce Th2 cells (Tao et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Th1/Th2 differentiation.

claim: At very high antigen doses, T cells revert to Th2 differentiation, potentially due to the susceptibility of Th1 cells to activation induced cell death (AICD).
source: Nevertheless, at very high antigen doses, T cells revert to Th2 differentiation, potentially due to the susceptibility of Th1 cells to activation induced cell death (AICD) (Hosken et al., 1995; Bretscher et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on antigen dose effects and AICD.

claim: AICD of Th1 cells might contribute to biased Tfh generation at the higher end of TCR signal strength during Clone-13 infection.
source: AICD of Th1 cells might also contribute to biased Tfh generation at the higher end of TCR signal strength during Clone-13 infection (Lohman and Welsh, 1998; Schorer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to studies on AICD during LCMV infection.

claim: The shift of relatively high affinity CD4 T cells toward a Tfh cell phenotype during Clone-13 infection is well documented.
source: The shift of relatively high affinity CD4 T cells toward a Tfh cell phenotype during Clone-13 infection is well documented (Fahey et al., 2011; Vella et al., 2017; Snell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CD4 T cell differentiation during Clone-13 infection.

claim: Clone-13 presents an altered inflammatory environment which contributes to an IFN stimulated gene signature and IL-10 production by chronically activated CD4 T cells.
source: In addition to antigen persistence, however, Clone-13 presents an altered inflammatory environment which contributes to an IFN stimulated gene signature and IL-10 production by chronically activated CD4 T cells (Crawford et al., 2014; Parish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on the inflammatory environment during Clone-13 infection.

claim: Activation of T cells in the presence of IFNα induces T cell secretion of IL-10 which is positively regulated by TCR signal strength.
source: For example, activation of T cells in the presence of IFNα induces T cell secretion of IL-10 which is positively regulated by TCR signal strength (Corre et al., 2013; Saraiva et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IFNα and IL-10 production.

claim: Blocking IFNα or IL-10 during Clone-13 infection rescues the Th1 effector compartment and improves viral control.
source: Consistent with this idea, blocking IFNα or IL-10 during Clone-13 infection rescues the Th1 effector compartment and improves viral control, although this likely depends on the rate of viral replication (Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013; Richter et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cytokine blocking during chronic infection.

claim: T cell production of IL-10 during chronic infection depends on sustained, but ERK-independent TCR signals.
source: Of particular interest, T cell production of IL-10 during chronic infection depends on sustained, but ERK-independent TCR signals, suggesting that inflammatory versus suppressive cytokine secretion may have distinct TCR signaling requirements (Parish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on TCR signaling and IL-10 production.

claim: The ability of weakly activated T cells to maintain a higher proportion of Th1 effectors might ultimately contribute to viral control.
source: Finally, the ability of weakly activated T cells to maintain a higher proportion of Th1 effectors might ultimately contribute to viral control.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed phenotype of weakly activated T cells.

claim: The weakest Clone-13 variant, Y72F, elicited significantly more expansion than its Armstrong counterpart.
source: The observation that the weakest Clone-13 variant, Y72F, elicited significantly more expansion than its Armstrong counterpart demonstrates that prolonged antigen presentation supports the accumulation of relatively low affinity T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing cell count data between Clone-13 Y72F and Armstrong Y72F infections.

claim: Prolonged antigen presentation supports the accumulation of relatively low affinity T cells.
source: The observation that the weakest Clone-13 variant, Y72F, elicited significantly more expansion than its Armstrong counterpart demonstrates that prolonged antigen presentation supports the accumulation of relatively low affinity T cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Y72F Clone-13 induces more expansion than Y72F Armstrong.

claim: Low affinity T cells comprise up to half of the endogenous effector T cell response.
source: Importantly, our study only follows the differentiation of T cells specific for a single epitope, while low affinity T cells are demonstrated to comprise up to half of the endogenous effector T cell response (Martinez et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on T cell affinity diversity.

claim: The rLCMV Clone-13 used in this study, which expresses WE-GP, tends to establish viremia for 20–30 days.
source: It should be noted that the rLCMV Clone-13 used in our study, which expresses WE-GP, tends to establish viremia for 20–30 days, which is somewhat less extensive than commonly observed for LCMV Clone-13 (Fallet et al., 2016; Sommerstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing rLCMV Clone-13 WE-GP.

claim: The duration of wild type Clone-13 viremia can vary considerably between animal facilities.
source: Although the duration of wild type Clone-13 viremia can vary considerably between animal facilities, it is possible that the Th bias we report here might have been even more pronounced if a more persistent LCMV variant had been used.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about variability in Clone-13 infection outcomes.

claim: The Th bias reported might have been even more pronounced if a more persistent LCMV variant had been used.
source: Although the duration of wild type Clone-13 viremia can vary considerably between animal facilities, it is possible that the Th bias we report here might have been even more pronounced if a more persistent LCMV variant had been used.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting that a more persistent virus might enhance the observed effects.

claim: Both Armstrong- and Clone-13-based viruses were equipped with the identical glycoprotein of the WE strain.
source: To exclude a potential impact of differential glycoprotein-mediated viral tropism on CD4 T cell differentiation, we equipped both the Armstrong- and Clone-13-based viruses with the identical glycoprotein of the WE strain and introduced the epitope mutations therein (resulting viruses referred to as rLCMV Armstrong and rLCMV Clone-13, respectively) (Bergthaler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of virus construction methods.

claim: The epitope mutations were introduced into the WE glycoprotein.
source: To exclude a potential impact of differential glycoprotein-mediated viral tropism on CD4 T cell differentiation, we equipped both the Armstrong- and Clone-13-based viruses with the identical glycoprotein of the WE strain and introduced the epitope mutations therein (resulting viruses referred to as rLCMV Armstrong and rLCMV Clone-13, respectively) (Bergthaler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of virus construction methods.

claim: GP61 wt has an EC50 of approximately 5 nM.
source: EC50 values are ~5 nM for GP61 wt, ~0.1 µM for V71S, and ~1 µM for Y72F.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide dose-activation curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SMARTA is a widely used TCR transgenic mouse line that mirrors the endogenous, immunodominant CD4 T cell response to LCMV.
source: These strains were used to assess the dynamics and differentiation of SMARTA T cells, a widely used TCR tg mouse line that mirrors the endogenous, immunodominant CD4 T cell response to LCMV (Oxenius et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the SMARTA TCR transgenic line.
